findings.title: Storage failure is recorded in the legacy duration metric
findings.body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), a failure in `d.Storage.Create` / `d.Storage.Update` is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Storage errors are therefore attributed to the legacy histogram, which skews the metrics that are meant to be compared when migrating between modes.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
findings.body: In the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `recordStorageDuration` rather than `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are mixed into the storage series and the legacy series gets no data for delete-collection.

findings.title: Delete success metric uses `name` as the kind label
findings.body: `recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This creates a metric label per object name, which is high cardinality, and splits the success series from the error series for the same method.

findings.title: Delete stores the wrong logger in the context
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` ignores the `log` built with name, kind and method values on the previous line. Downstream storage logging loses that context, unlike every other method in the file, which uses `log`.

findings.title: Async legacy writes reuse the request context and are not detached from it
findings.body: The goroutines derive their timeout context from the request `ctx`. Once the HTTP handler returns, that context is cancelled, so the legacy write is typically cancelled before or during execution, and the failure is only recorded as a metric. The same applies in Update, Delete and DeleteCollection. The "safe measure" legacy write is therefore unreliable. The code needs `context.WithoutCancel` or a fresh background context, with the values it needs copied over.

findings.title: Async legacy Update/Create reuse objects and objInfo after the request returns
findings.body: The goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Update` with the original `objInfo`, and Create passes the original `obj`. Both were already used or mutated by the storage write, and `objInfo.UpdatedObject` is re-evaluated against the legacy object concurrently with the request path. The previous code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper` so legacy received the exact object stored in unified storage. Now legacy may compute a different result, and there is a data race on the shared request objects. The legacy write is also not ordered across consecutive updates, so older writes can land after newer ones.

findings.title: Redundant `return created, err` after the err != nil check
findings.body: After the early return on error, `err` is always nil. Returning `created, err` (also in Update and Delete) is misleading, and `return created, nil` is clearer.

findings.title: Tests don't verify the async legacy write and race with mock use
findings.body: The tests never assert that the legacy store is called after a successful storage write, and they don't wait for the goroutines. Legacy mock calls can happen after the test ends, and `mock.Mock` is shared between the storage and legacy mocks. Legacy expectations are set up but never verified, so a regression where legacy is never written would pass. The error cases for Create set a legacy expectation that is never used.

findings.title: Redundant per-test registry shadows the package-level one
findings.body: TestMode3_Get creates a new `prometheus.NewRegistry()` that shadows the package-level `p`, while the other tests use `p`. This is inconsistent. The Mode1 test had the same line removed in this PR.
